title: Making New Elements
objective: After this level you can explain how the heaviest elements are made in laboratories.
summary: Elements beyond uranium are made by people, starting with neptunium in 1940. Element 118 came from fusing calcium (20 protons) with californium (98). The 2016 names completed row seven.

cards.headline: Past uranium, element 92, nature almost runs out.
cards.body: Every element beyond uranium was first made by people, in reactors and particle accelerators. Only two of them turn up in nature, in tiny traces. So how do you build an element nobody has ever seen?

cards.headline: Neptunium: one step past uranium
cards.body: In 1940, Edwin McMillan and Philip Abelson at Berkeley bombarded uranium with neutrons and made element 93. They named it neptunium, after Neptune, the planet beyond Uranus, just as their element sat beyond uranium. Elements past uranium are called transuranium elements. All 26 known today are radioactive.

cards.fact: Element 118 was made by fusing calcium (20 protons) with californium (98).
cards.context: In 2005, in Dubna, Russia, a Russian and American team fired calcium ions at a californium target at about 10 percent of the speed of light. Remember Level 21: the proton count decides the element. Nuclei almost never fuse, but when they did, 20 plus 98 made 118. From February to June, the experiment produced three atoms.

cards.headline: The seventh row, complete
cards.body: In 2016, IUPAC named the four newest elements: nihonium (113), moscovium (115), tennessine (117) and oganesson (118), completing the table's seventh row. Oganesson honors Yuri Oganessian, a pioneer of superheavy element research, who was alive to see it. Only a few atoms of oganesson have ever been made. Don't expect an oganesson ring.

cards.headline: New elements: built
learned: Transuranium elements lie beyond uranium, element 92

options.label: Elements that glow in the dark
options.rationale: Glowing has nothing to do with the name.

options.label: The lightest elements, made first
options.rationale: They are the heaviest, not the lightest.

options.label: Metals that don't react with water
options.rationale: The name is about position, not reactions.

questions.explanation: Trans means beyond: these are the elements past uranium, all radioactive.

questions.prompt: A calcium nucleus (20 protons) fused with californium (98 protons). Why was the result element 118?

options.label: The proton count sets the element: 20 + 98 = 118
Their masses added up to exactly 118
options.rationale: The element is set by protons, not by mass.

options.label: Calcium turns into whatever it hits
options.rationale: Calcium has no such power; the protons simply add up.

options.label: The beam's speed picked the element
options.rationale: Speed helps nuclei fuse, but protons decide the element.

questions.explanation: An element is defined by its atomic number, so 20 protons plus 98 protons makes element 118.

questions.prompt: Level 23 said the table has 7 rows. What did naming elements 113, 115, 117 and 118 in 2016 do?

options.label: It added an eighth row
options.rationale: No eighth-row element has been named.

options.label: It removed four old elements
options.rationale: Nothing was removed; four were added.

options.label: It swapped two groups
options.rationale: The groups stayed as they were.

questions.explanation: IUPAC's 2016 names filled the last gaps in the seventh row.
